title: The Kernel's Write: Application Read-Only Memory
event_hint: AROM (Application Read-Only Memory): a proposed hardware/software interface for LtRAM (Long-term RAM, e.g. RRAM/PCM/FeFET/MRAM) that makes LtRAM pages read-only to applications and offloads wear-leveling/migration to the OS, prototyped on Enzian with NOR flash.
problem: DRAM is now over half of server cost (Microsoft Azure, Meta) and its cost-per-bit has plateaued. LtRAM (denser, cheaper emerging memory competing with DRAM read latency) has three drawbacks - asymmetric read/write latency, limited endurance, coarse write granularity. Intel Optane tried to hide these with an on-DIMM translation layer (AIT, wear-leveling, read/write caching) that added significant latency and cost, eroding the advantage.
mechanism: AROM enforces that LtRAM pages are read-only to applications and written only by the OS during page migrations, using copy-on-write (CoW): application writes to LtRAM trigger a fault that migrates the page back to DRAM before the store applies. This lets the DIMM controller drop the Address Indirection Table (AIT), its DRAM cache, and hardware wear-leveling; the controller does cache-line reads and 4KB page writes and exposes cell-health metadata, while the OS handles placement, migration and wear-leveling (token allocator). Goal: match pure-DRAM performance on read-mostly workloads while capturing LtRAM density/cost.

evidence.claim: DRAM accounts for over half of total server cost at Microsoft Azure and Meta, and DRAM cost-per-bit has plateaued over the past decade.
evidence.condition: Microsoft Azure and Meta datacenter reports

evidence.claim: Intel Optane's controller mechanisms impose measurable overheads: a read-modify-write on every sub-256B store, an AIT lookup on every read, a 160x tail-latency spike from internal wear-leveling migrations, and a bandwidth collapse under mixed read/write workloads; cache-line/4KB-page granularity mismatch caused a 75% write throughput drop and 2x random-read latency.
evidence.value: 160x tail-latency spike; 75% write throughput drop; 2x random-read latency
evidence.source_locator: Evidence locator: PDF Page 2 - 3.2 Case Study: Intel Optane; PDF Page 3 - Table

evidence.claim: AROM removes the AIT and its ~75 ns media access incurred on the 94% of random reads that miss the AIT cache, plus ~60 us tail-latency spikes from hardware-driven wear-leveling migrations; only intrinsic media access latency remains.
evidence.value: ~75 ns AIT-miss overhead; ~60 us tail spikes
evidence.baseline: Optane AIT-cache-miss path and hardware wear-leveling

evidence.claim: Representative LtRAM technology parameters (shape, not precision): DRAM 80ns read/80ns write/infinite endurance; 3D V-RRAM 100ns/1us/10^6; 3D FeFET 200ns/10us/10^5; PCM 300ns/1us/10^8 (256B write); STT-MRAM 20ns/20ns/10^15 (word write, high cost/bit).

Prototyped on the Enzian research platform (48x ARM v8 CPU + coherent FPGA as LtRAM controller, Linux 6.8 with page-migration extensions) using a 256 MB Micron Serial NOR Flash device; measured chip latencies 490 ns for 128B read, 16 us for 256B write, 18 ms for 4KB erase; NOR chosen for availability (10^5 erase cycles/block), not as a canonical LtRAM technology.

evaluation_context: Position/architecture paper with a research-platform prototype, not a performance benchmark study. Prototype hardware: Enzian (48x ARM v8 + cache-coherent FPGA) with a 256 MB Micron Serial NOR Flash device acting as LtRAM via an FPGA controller, running Linux kernel 6.8 with custom page-migration extensions. LtRAM candidate parameters surveyed (Table 1) are described as shape, not precise, and can shift by orders of magnitude with material/circuit choices. No standard application-level benchmark throughput/latency results are presented.
limitations: The authors explicitly state 'Application-level benchmark evaluation remains future work.' Only chip-level prototype latencies (NOR flash on Enzian) are reported; there are no end-to-end workload performance, cost/bit, or endurance-wear measurements under realistic datacenter applications. Several core policies are left open: ideal LtRAM technology, best migration policy, best wear-leveling strategy, and preventing OOM faults during write-heavy phase changes. NOR flash is used for prototyping convenience, not as the intended deployment medium, and its 10^5 erase cycles and ms erase latency are far from production LtRAM targets.
project_relevance: AROM is relevant to the storage-media question of whether non-volatile emerging memory (LtRAM: RRAM/PCM/FeFET/MRAM) can move into the main-memory tier for read-mostly data (code pages, ML inference weights, Redis/Memcached). It argues the interface - not the media - is the bottleneck, and proposes an OS-managed CoW abstraction. For the project card it is an early-stage interface proposal with a research prototype, not a deployable product or measured system gain; cost/density benefits are projected, not demonstrated at application level.
source_notes: arXiv preprint 2606.26138v1 (18 Jun 2026), FETCHED primary source; authors from Stanford University.
This is an architecture/interface proposal with an Enzian+NOR-flash prototype; the authors explicitly defer application-level benchmark evaluation to future work.

Optane overhead numbers (160x tail spike, 75% write throughput drop, 2x random-read latency, ~75 ns AIT-miss, ~60 us wear-leveling spike) are attributed to prior Optane experimental studies, not measured in this paper.
